# Applications: VERT Wearable for Athletes

## Where this applies

- Inference: Jump-count monitoring for Baylor volleyball or basketball practice. The speaker described setting a jump count cap per practice, citing USA Volleyball stopping players at a threshold [16:07]. Athletic Performance could trial a per-practice jump count for a high-volume position or drill.
- Inference: Using jump height from a waist sensor as a within-athlete trend over a season, as a player described tracking whether height changes [23:17]. At Baylor this would sit beside force plate CMJ, not replace it.
- Inference: Training-session leaderboards as motivation, such as the 30 inch club the speaker described [13:01]. A football equivalent might be a visible, opt-in board for a single jump or sprint metric during off-season sessions.
- Inference: Reading player load style output (the speaker's g-force and accumulated g-force) alongside existing GPS load in a sport with no GPS coverage [19:42].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ on ForceDecks was chosen as the daily readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable. The talk offers jump height from a wearable as a similar objective jump metric [20:12]; it does not offer a reactive strength measure, so it extends nothing on mRSI.
- Eric's baseline: Core GPS metrics include player load and IMA for indoor sessions without GPS coverage, with Catapult and Kitman Labs as the stack. The talk's g-force and acceleration measure [18:42] overlaps in purpose, but the speaker gave no validity or reliability data against Catapult.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and a valid test is still wrong if it cannot be collected consistently at scale. The talk is silent on compliance cost; its examples are small groups.
- Eric's baseline: Reduce injury risk through progression, not claim to prevent it. The speaker said managing jump numbers lets coaches stop before "something really happens" [16:07], and cited player emails thanking the product for staying healthy [16:38]. That is closer to a prevention claim than the baseline allows; no injury data was shown.

## What would have to be true

- Evidence that waist-worn jump height agrees with ForceDecks CMJ jump height in Baylor athletes (the talk gave none).
- A reason to believe a jump count threshold relates to injury; the talk gave only a pitch count analogy [15:36] and a practice cap of about 100 as an example.
- Staff ownership and a data home (Kitman Labs) before adding another device.

## Do not apply when

- The sport or drill has little jumping, so jump count carries little signal.
- The point is injury prevention and no injury or soreness outcome is tracked; testimonials are not evidence.
- Fan-facing or broadcast display of athlete data (the talk's main product line) would put athlete performance data in public view; Baylor would need athlete consent and compliance review first.
- The speaker is the company founder, so efficacy claims are a commercial view.

## First step

Have one sports staff member wear no new device; instead, count jumps per practice by hand or from video for one volleyball practice week, and compare with the 100 jump figure the speaker mentioned, to see whether a count cap would ever be reached.

The speaker described setting a jump count cap per practice, citing USA Volleyball stopping players at a threshold [16:07]. Athletic Performance could trial a per-practice jump count for a high-volume position or drill.
- Inference: Using jump height from a waist sensor as a within-athlete trend over a season, as a player described tracking whether height changes [23:17]. At Baylor this would sit beside force plate CMJ, not replace it.
- Inference: Training-session leaderboards as motivation, such as the 30 inch club the speaker described [13:01]. A football equivalent might be a visible, opt-in board for a single jump or sprint metric during off-season sessions.
- Inference: Reading player load style output (the speaker's g-force and accumulated g-force) alongside existing GPS load in a sport with no GPS coverage [19:42].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ on ForceDecks was chosen as the daily readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable. The talk offers jump height from a wearable as a similar objective jump metric [20:12]; it does not offer a reactive strength measure, so it extends nothing on mRSI.
- Eric's baseline: Core GPS metrics include player load and IMA for indoor sessions without GPS coverage, with Catapult and Kitman Labs as the stack. The talk's g-force and acceleration measure [18:42] overlaps in purpose, but the speaker gave no validity or reliability data against Catapult.

- Eric's baseline: Reduce injury risk through progression, not claim to prevent it. The speaker said managing jump numbers lets coaches stop before "something really happens" [16:07], and cited player emails thanking the product for staying healthy [16:38]. That is closer to a prevention claim than the baseline allows; no injury data was shown.

## What would have to be true

- Evidence that waist-worn jump height agrees with ForceDecks CMJ jump height in Baylor athletes (the talk gave none).
- A reason to believe a jump count threshold relates to injury; the talk gave only a pitch count analogy [15:36] and a practice cap of about 100 as an example.
- Staff ownership and a data home (Kitman Labs) before adding another device.

## Do not apply when

- The sport or drill has little jumping, so jump count carries little signal.
- The point is injury prevention and no injury or soreness outcome is tracked; testimonials are not evidence.
- Fan-facing or broadcast display of athlete data (the talk's main product line) would put athlete performance data in public view; Baylor would need athlete consent and compliance review first.
- The speaker is the company founder, so efficacy claims are a commercial view.

## First step

Have one sports staff member wear no new device; instead, count jumps per practice by hand or from video for one volleyball practice week, and compare with the 100 jump figure the speaker mentioned, to see whether a count cap would ever be reached.

=== FILE: videos/2016-04-02_LkNYHpC82yc_sports-performance-measurement-and-analytics/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: LkNYHpC82yc
title: "SSAC16: Sports Performance  Measurement and Analytics"
event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Dr Lorena Martin (caption spelling, named by the host)]
topics: [sports-science, american-football, basketball, injury-health, other-sport:tennis]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The speaker argues that sports data scientists need subject matter knowledge, including basic physiology, because athletes differ by sport and by position, and so should the way they are measured. She compares NFL and NBA combine results by position, questions whether single tests (the bench press especially) suit every position, and presents a measurement model with physical, physiological, psychological, behavioral and environmental variables. She briefly describes a tennis pilot on narcissism and calls for individualized "precision athleticism" using wearables, borrowed from precision medicine. The talk is a broad survey drawn from her new book, with few numbers and no validation data.

## Key claims

- Data scientists in sport should be able to discuss their sport as a fan would, not only the numbers [02:05].
- Muscle fiber type is partly genetic and partly trained; type one fibers resist fatigue but give less power and force, type two the reverse [04:37].
- The three energy systems are phosphagen, glycogen and oxidative; a maximal sprint relies on the first only briefly before speed drops [06:42, 07:14].
- Between sports, and between positions within a sport, athletes should be assessed and trained differently [10:16].
- NFL combine results differ by position, shown with a simple ANOVA on public data [13:52].
- The bench press may not suit some positions; she asked whether a quarterback should be tested on it at all and said she was only posing questions [13:52].
- Height is not the best predictor in basketball; wingspan and hand size are better [17:00].
- Psychological variables are often neglected and should be measured, but available scales are self-reported and biased [19:34, 20:05].
- Outliers should be studied, not just removed [23:07].
- Treatment should be individualized ("n of one") using wearables, as in precision medicine [27:13].
- Psychological variables can be trained, with some harder to change than others [30:15].

## Numbers and definitions

- Seven to eight muscle fiber types exist, simplified to type one and type two [03:36].
- Phosphagen system dominates the first five to 10 seconds of a maximal effort [06:42].
- Work to rest ratios of "1:3, 1:2, 1:20" are mentioned [08:15]; the captions are garbled and the intended ratios cannot be confirmed.
- NFL combine bench press is at 225 pounds; centers reached about 35 to 40 reps [13:21].
- NBA draft bench press is at 185 pounds, with results up to five, 10 or 15 reps [15:27, 15:59].
- "Load" here means resistance weight, not wearable load [15:59].
- Muscular strength is maximum force in one repetition; muscular endurance is maximum repetitions [13:21].
- Brady is cited as winning four out of six Super Bowls, as an outlier example [23:07].

## Methods and frameworks named

- ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests (normality assumed) on public combine data, in R [11:18, 13:52].
- A measurement model with her colleague: physical variables (strength, power, endurance, flexibility, reaction time, coordination, body composition, specific skills), physiological (lactate threshold, resting heart rate, blood pressure, VO2 max, glucose and insulin, injury history, telomere length, methylome), psychological, behavioral and environmental [17:31, 18:31, 19:03].
- Implicit association task to probe confidence versus narcissism by reaction time latency [21:05, 22:05].
- Precision medicine framing, "n of one" trials, time varying covariates [27:13, 27:44].

## Limits and open questions

- The tennis pilot gave no sample size, results or validation [20:35 to 22:05].
- Combine position comparisons are not tied to game performance or to injury.
- Self-report measures are acknowledged as biased [20:05]; the implicit task was shown only as a similar example.
- The cryotherapy, stem cell and gene editing remarks are loose and not evidenced [24:39, 26:43].
- Claim that the injury risk of a quarterback tested on the bench press is raised is explicitly not asserted [13:52].
- Book promotion and commercial thanks to a sponsor appear at [28:14].

## Q&A

- A question on how the data would be used: she would use it for injury prevention, baselines and response to training [29:14].
- Can psychological variables be modified: yes, with willingness, though some are harder [29:44, 30:15].
- Self-reports and big data: patterns may become clearer, and self-efficacy, confidence and narcissism need better objective models, which she called a call to action [31:19, 31:50].

event: SSAC16 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)

topics: [sports-science, injury-health, basketball, other-sport:volleyball]
confidence: untested

## Summary

The founder of a jump-measuring wearable describes his company's path from a waist-worn device that reports jump height and jump count to broadcast use (VERT Cast) and a new device that adds g-force and acceleration. He argues the same data serve fans, motivation, performance and injury prevention. Examples come mostly from volleyball: televised jump numbers, a 30 inch club for motivation, and a jump count cap in USA Volleyball practice. This is a company pitch with testimonials, not a study; no validity, reliability or injury data are shown.

## Key claims

- A waist-worn device logs jump height and count and syncs to an app [01:46].
- Jump count is an unmeasured load in volleyball and basketball, comparable to pitch count in baseball [06:21].
- Real-time jump data on Jumbotron and TV can drive fan engagement [07:54, 12:31].
- Public milestones (the 30 inch club) motivate athletes [13:01, 13:32].
- Coaches can set a jump count limit per practice; USA Volleyball players stop at a certain number to avoid overdoing it [16:07].
- Players have written to him saying they stayed healthy because of the product [16:38]; no data were shown.
- Step counts say little; measuring g-force of each movement says more about effort [19:12, 19:42].
- Combining jump, g-force and heart rate gives an idea of an athlete's condition [20:43].
- Future focus is recovery, looking at surges and jerk [22:16].
- A private mode keeps team data on the team's own servers [21:44].

## Numbers and definitions

- Wearables market expected to reach "$40 billion" by "20121" (garbled year) [04:49].
- Coaches notice jumps of 35 or 40 inches [05:51].
- Example in-game jumps of 32 inches [08:26] and 28.6 inches with seven kills [08:56]; top tournament jump 34 inches, later 34 and a half [10:59, 12:00].
- A player averaging 27 inches with best of 38 [10:29].
- 103 jumps shown on a coach screen; a practice cap of about 100 suggested; pitch count example of 58 [15:05, 15:36].
- Example g-force readings: 8.3 g peak; cycling example 3.2 rising to 4.1 [20:12].
- Heart rate of 110 during a convention [20:43].
- First NBA client the Miami Heat; first used in a game the week before [21:13, 21:44].
- Built "in about two years" [24:49]; USA men's team win after 30 years [24:19].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Wearable jump and g-force sensor with app, team system (VERT Coach) for multiple sensors, VERT Cast broadcast feed [15:05, 02:18].
- Jump count thresholds per position and drill [15:36].

## Limits and open questions

- No accuracy, reliability or validity data for jump height or g-force.
- Injury prevention is supported by testimonials only [16:38]; no outcome data.
- The USA volleyball medal results are credited loosely and are not evidence of a product effect [24:19].
- Speaker is the company founder; all claims are commercial.
- Several names (players, coaches) are garbled in captions and not repeated here.

## Q&A

- None; the talk ends at [24:49] with a closing remark and applause.

## Summary

Two vendor presenters introduce a near-field indoor tracking system for hockey and basketball, built after a team owner asked why GPS could not be used indoors. The system records position and speed and merges them with video and physiology monitors into video-centric reports, shown on screens or a Jumbotron as motivation. Most of the talk is the engineering pitch and a long Q&A on accuracy, subject limits, league approval and football fields. No team data are shown. It is a product description, with vendor-stated precision and no independent validation.

## Key claims

- Athlete monitoring makes workload and fatigue visible and may help prevent injury [04:29].
- Injury prediction is hard because of luck and missing covariates, in the lead speaker's view [04:59].
- Outdoor GPS companies struggle indoors with accuracy and obstruction [07:03].
- Near-field technology is not affected by line of sight, bunching or head position [09:08].
- Coaches already study video, so metrics should appear synchronized with video [05:29, 10:42].
- Live display of speed and velocity motivates players in training [13:17, 17:24].
- A virtual private network can let offsite clinicians review a player's metrics, but cloud servers are not recommended [14:48].
- The system is not approved for league games [23:05].

## Numbers and definitions

- Introduced in 2012; tested at The Edge Sports Center and at Boston University in 2013; system at the Honda Center from September [05:59, 06:31].
- 13 direct measurements [09:39, 10:11].
- Tag size of a pack of wooden matches, 3 to four hour duty cycle [11:15].
- Precision of 30 cm at 10 Hz [18:59].
- Limits of 20 subjects for hockey and 15 for basketball; a marching band test tracked 400 subjects at five Hertz [22:03, 22:34].
- Range: about a hockey rink of 200 by 95; a thousand yard track tried the previous week [24:36, 25:08].
- 2D capture currently, 3D planned [16:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Near-field electromagnetic tag with three-axis antenna, claimed to work through walls [19:59, 20:30].
- Synchronized capture of video, computer-generated animation, biometrics from third-party monitors, and a metrics panel [08:35, 12:16].
- Reports by line, shift, time in zone [13:47].

## Limits and open questions

- No team results shown (the speaker explained a team's data could not be shared) [12:47].
- Accuracy claim is the vendor's; no validation study cited.
- Claim of superiority to accelerometer-based systems is unsupported [20:30].
- Football fields and indoor football were still under test [25:08, 25:38].
- Only one team can be tracked; whether both sides could be is a league decision [23:05].
- Caption inconsistency: company named "bioamp" at [00:22] and "biocam" later.

## Q&A

- Hardware dimensions: 2D capture now [16:51].
- Sport psychology use: motivation and feedback plus practice for learning [17:24, 17:55].
- Precision and sampling: 30 cm at 10 Hz [18:59].
- How it differs from competitors: near-field shortwave, video combined with workload [19:59, 20:30, 21:01].
- Only tagged subjects tracked [21:01].
- How many subjects: 20 hockey, 15 basketball [22:03].
- Both teams in games: league decision [23:05].
- Tag type: shown against a coin [24:05].
- Venue size: rink sized, football fields planned [24:36, 25:08].
- Puck tracking: not practical, but grip and EMG were put in a stick [26:12, 26:44].

Caption problems: "20121" (VERT market year), the work-to-rest ratio in LkNYHpC82yc [08:15], and the company name "bioamp"/"biocam" are garbled; speaker names are caption spellings; one slip for review: in the l-m63eiixSE Q&A, the "coin" at [24:05] is captioned as "quarter" and the tag description there is partly inaudible.
